By
													Atlantic Council experts

The world’s finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering in Bangkok, Thailand this week for the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. Our experts are on the ground talking to leaders and getting the behind-the-scenes scoop on how the Bretton Woods institutions are taking on the most urgent challenges in the global economy, including conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, soaring public debt, and the impact of artificial intelligence (AI).

Check back for expert reactions to breaking news, updates from our events with high-level policymakers, and more.

To make the leap, Thailand needs to convert foreign investment into local capabilities

At a high-stakes meeting today, the G20 is searching for balance

Step into the ring with the Atlantic Council’s Josh Lipsky as he breaks down perhaps the biggest topic at the Annual Meetings—the pugnacious bond market—with the help of Thai fighters.

Almost thirty years after the Asian financial crisis engulfed the region in economic turmoil, South Korea and the Association of Southeast Asian Nation (ASEAN) economies have again become an important motor for the global economy. They are benefiting from a global super-cycle in AI investment, while a declining bilateral flow of goods between the US and China has increased trade flows through Asian economies more generally.

At the same time, the region is becoming more exposed to geopolitical developments. China is its largest production partner, a major source of capital and intermediate goods, and an important consumer market. On the other hand, the United States remains a critical export destination, technology provider, investor, and security partner. Neither relationship can substitute for the other, but deteriorating relations between the two superpowers could make it more difficult for the region to keep its current dynamic.

For South Korea, the AI boom has produced exceptional demand for semiconductors and helped offset the effects of higher energy prices. But as former Bank of Korea Governor Changyong Rhee noted during an Atlantic Council discussion this week in Bangkok, the gains are concentrated in a few companies and partly reflect US restrictions on China’s access to advanced semiconductor equipment. China’s eventual technological progress—or a relaxation of these restrictions—could weaken South Korea’s current advantage.

China’s economic role is also changing. South Korean companies have benefited for many years from supplying and investing in the “factory of Asia.” However, Beijing’s export-oriented economic model means that South Korean companies are now confronting Chinese companies at home and abroad.

ASEAN economies face a related dilemma. Owing mainly to Chinese investment and inexpensive inputs, they have become tightly integrated into global supply chains. Yet new investment does not automatically create domestic capabilities: much of the underlying research and technology is still under foreign control.

The region may also face increased financial volatility. Rhee described how rapid gains in semiconductor shares increased foreign investors’ exposure to the South Korean market. Their subsequent portfolio rebalancing generated equity sales and purchases of dollars, putting downward pressure on the won even as South Korea’s current-account surplus expanded.

This complicates the distinction between strong and weak external positions, and memories of the 1997 crisis can make them difficult to accept. Countries therefore may face a choice between allowing the exchange rate to absorb external shocks and limiting its volatility, which could put unwanted constraints on monetary policy.

The region’s dependency on oil imports also means that higher prices could weaken trade balances and raise inflation, while shifts in the global risk appetite could generate capital outflows and exchange-rate pressures. Currency depreciation could complicate trade relations with the United States, and central banks would have a harder job weighing their price stability objective against the impact of policy decisions on the domestic economy.

To improve the foundations for stable economic growth, former Indonesian Finance Minister Chatib Basri at an Atlantic Council event this week called for domestic industry to collaborate with external partners across geopolitical camps. He pointed to a recent partnership between the Ford Motor Company, China’s Huayou Cobalt, and Vale Indonesia that could help Indonesia upgrade its nickel processing capabilities.

Sutapa Amornvivat, a Thai leader in digital integration, suggested that the digital economy offered another route to stronger economic growth. ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement, due to be signed in November, could have a catalytic impact as it promotes digital payments and e-commerce more broadly.

First, however, ASEAN countries must decide how to combine competing technologies, data rules, security standards, and AI systems without dividing the regional market. They also would have to manage wide differences in digital infrastructure, energy availability, and skills across member states. Growing integration would indeed help the region to prepare for a turn in the economic cycle. Deepening trade under the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), moving toward interoperable payment systems, and improving energy networks could give East and Southeast Asian firms access to a market large enough to support innovation and real economies of scale, helping them to consolidate their gains if and when the economic cycle turns again.

These days, central banks are asked to solve an inflation problem they did not create and cannot solve alone. From my observations here at the Annual Meetings, central bankers are not particularly happy about this. In any conversation in hallways and meeting rooms about inflation’s resurgence, supply side factors are immediately mentioned—particularly by the monetary policy crowd.

The numbers tell the story. The IMF projects global headline inflation to rise from 4.1 percent in 2025 to 4.7 percent in 2026, with euro area inflation increasing from 2.1 to 3.1 percent and the US increasing from 2.7 to 3.6 percent.

This is partly driven by four factors that have nothing to do with monetary policy:

To fight back, central banks have essentially one weapon in their arsenal: interest rates. So they can only confront inflationary pressures by suppressing aggregate demand through higher interest rates. They cannot reduce tariffs, resolve conflicts, expand energy supplies, reverse subsidies, or reduce defense expenditures.

In today’s geoeconomically charged landscape, price stability can no longer be treated as the exclusive responsibility of central banks. While central banks’ independence and their leadership in the fight against inflation is essential, confronting inflation requires greater coordination across monetary, fiscal, trade, industrial, and foreign policies. Otherwise, governments risk fueling inflation with one set of policies while forcing central banks to fight it at the expense of investment, employment, and growth.

It is rare to have four economists agree on one policy priority for a country’s growth prospects. My conversation yesterday with Santitarn Sathirathai (vice minister of finance for Thailand), Stephen Ndegwa (World Bank division director for Thailand and Myanmar), and Arnaud Dupoizat (International Finance Corporation’s regional director for East Asia) was one of those rare occasions. When asked about one policy that tops their list of priorities in the next three to five years to help Thailand’s ambition in achieving high-income status by 2037, all three mentioned increasing productivity and domestic value added in the Thai economy—exactly my main finding a few weeks ago when I wrote “the measure of success should not be the amount of investment Thailand attracts, but the value it creates at home.”

This is true, not only for Thailand, but also for all Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) economies. The amounts of foreign trade relative to the size of these economies are some of the highest in the world. Foreign direct investment (FDI) has been fueling their industrial base, especially in the past decade because of “China + One” policies pursued by multinational companies. However, the share of domestic value added in ASEAN economies (especially the bigger economies known as the ASEAN-5: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam) has been shrinking, productivity has more or less stalled, and high-paying jobs have been scarce.

So, while more FDI is always welcomed, turning “that FDI into local capabilities, better [small and medium-sized enterprises], better skills, and better jobs,” as Santitarn put it, is what is most needed for Thailand and other ASEAN-5 economies for them to continue growing and avoid the middle-income trap.

Kerschyl Singh
    Bretton Woods 2.0 fellow at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center
  






While the IMF’s World Economic Outlook lays out resilient growth and inflation forecasts, the Global Financial Stability Report makes the detailed case around the risks and vulnerabilities in the outlook. Three themes are worth mentioning, and the key vulnerability is that all three have meaningful interaction with the bond market.
